title: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease: A case report and differential diagnoses
case_prompt:
A 65-year-old woman was referred with a 3-month history of behavioral and personality changes and progressive cognitive decline. Initially, she had increasing forgetfulness and difficulty with activities of daily living, which progressed to not recognizing family members. She later developed generalized stiffness and visual hallucinations, seeing random people. Over the 2 weeks before presentation, her condition worsened rapidly: she became unable to ambulate and had new urinary and fecal incontinence. She had no relevant past medical or psychiatric history and no family history of neurologic disease.

On examination, she was mute and appeared ill. There was increased muscle tone and brisk reflexes in all extremities, a prominent jaw jerk, bilateral palmomental reflexes, paratonia, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and intermittent forced eye gaze deviation. Continuous myoclonic jerks affected all limbs, and she was unable to stand because of ataxia.

Routine laboratory tests, including serology for hepatitis B, HIV, and syphilis, were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 2 lymphocytes per cubic millimeter, glucose 3.5 mmol/L, total protein 62 mg/dL, and adenosine deaminase 2.32 U/L. Thyroid function tests, vitamin B12, and folate levels were normal. Chest radiography, electrocardiography, and abdominal–pelvic ultrasonography were unremarkable.

Electroencephalography revealed continuous periodic complexes and generalized slow waves. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffusion-weighted high signal intensity in the bilateral frontal (right > left) and occipital cortices, and T2-weighted images showed subtle high signal in the pulvinar nuclei of the bilateral thalami, giving a “hockey-stick” appearance. An autoimmune encephalitis panel, including antibodies against NMDA, AMPA (GluR1 and GluR2), GABA-B, LGI1, and CASPR2 receptors, was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Autoimmune encephalitis — “Autoimmune encephalitis panel … was found to be negative.”  
2. Hashimoto's encephalopathy — “Hashimoto's encephalopathy may have a relapsing–remitting course with stroke‐like symptoms; meanwhile, the course of sCJD is fulminant, leading to death within 1‐year time in 85% of patients.”  
3. Vascular pathologies — “Symptoms typically present in vascular pathologies like headache and localizing motor; visual or sensory signs were absent in our case. She had no risk factors for vascular diseases as well as a normal coagulation profile.”  
4. Other dementias (Alzheimer’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, corticobasal degeneration) — “It must be differentiated from other dementias such as Alzheimer’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and corticobasal degeneration, which are also associated with myoclonus and have a more rapid course.”  
5. Paraneoplastic syndrome — “Other differential diagnoses include paraneoplastic syndrome and autoimmune encephalitis making neuroimaging and CSF analysis essential.”  
6. Infectious causes — “Routine laboratory investigations including serology for hepatitis B, HIV, and syphilis were all negative.”  
7. Toxic/metabolic causes — “Thyroid hormones, vitamin B12, and folate levels were all within normal limits.”  
8. Other causes of rapidly progressive dementia — “Before proceeding with the diagnosis, we ruled out many other vascular/ischemic, infectious, toxic/metabolic, autoimmune, metastatic/neoplasm related, iatrogenic, systemic/seizures/sarcoid, and demyelinating causes of rapidly progressive dementia, on the basis of clinical presentation and best utilizing some investigations available in our setting.”
